strengths: Introduces a clean, well-motivated notion of group fairness for optimal transport (the F-fair coupling), which requires the group-to-group marginals of the transport plan to match a central planner's target. This is modular enough to encode quotas, anti-homogamy, and diversity goals, and is a genuinely new angle for fairness in matching/OT.

The dual characterization (Proposition 3.3) is elegant and correctly yields a Sinkhorn-style algorithm (FairSinkhorn) with a simple projection step; the derivation in Appendix A is correct and the algorithm is a natural, practical modification of Sinkhorn.

The sample complexity result for fairness-penalized entropic OT (Theorem 4.2), claimed to match the 1/sqrt(n) rate of unpenalized entropic OT and to extend to generic convex penalties, is a theoretically interesting contribution if correct.

The cost-learning approach via bilevel optimization is a novel and useful idea, and Theorem 4.4 gives a uniform-in-theta deviation bound that supports reusing the learned cost on unseen data—addressing a real practical limitation of the penalized approach.
The related-work discussion is thoughtful and correctly positions the work relative to OT-for-fairness, Wasserstein-barycenter fairness, and constrained OT literature.
The problem motivation (school assignment, dating apps, kidney exchange) is compelling and the ethical framing is appropriate.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is thin: all experiments use synthetic 2D data (Gaussian mixtures and concentric circles). No real-world or higher-dimensional dataset is used, despite the motivation being entirely about real applications (school admissions, dating, etc.). This limits the significance and reach of the empirical claims.

No comparison against existing fairness-in-matching or fair-OT baselines. The only reference points are the authors' own methods and the unconstrained Sinkhorn plan, so it is impossible to gauge whether the proposed trade-offs are competitive.

Presentation problems: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 are essentially duplicated ('Approaches and Metrics' appears twice with near-identical text), which is a clear proofreading failure. The experiments section also cites 'Theorem 4.1' and 'Theorem 4.2' where it should cite Example 4.1/4.2, and Figure 3's caption says 'de Mahalanobis'.

The appendix proofs are difficult to verify as written: the proof of Theorem 4.2 contains a badly garbled block of nested \vbox/\overbrace LaTeX that is unreadable, the rate is written as 'O(1/sqrt(n)^{-1})' (a typo), and the statement of Assumption 4.1/the theorem in the main text (infinitely differentiable) differs from the appendix (L-Lipschitz and infinitely differentiable) with no dependence on L shown. This raises concerns about the rigor of the central theoretical claims.

The cost-learning approach is non-convex with no optimization guarantees, and the authors explicitly leave a generalization bound for it to future work. The gap between the (strong) deviation bound of Theorem 4.4 and the (uncontrolled) quality of the learned cost is not discussed.

The fairness definition amounts to imposing linear marginal constraints on the group-group coupling; while useful, it is close in spirit to constrained OT, and the paper does not sharply articulate why this specific constraint family is more than a natural extension of existing constrained-OT formulations.

Reproducibility is limited: code is promised only upon publication, and key experimental details (e.g., how the Pareto fronts are constructed, the exact fairness target construction in Figure 3/5, seeds/variance across runs) are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: enforcing group-level fairness in optimal-transport-based matching, with concrete motivating examples (school assignment, dating apps) and a clear gap relative to prior work that mostly uses OT as a tool for fair prediction rather than constraining the OT plan itself.

The proposed fairness notion (an F-fair coupling, i.e., prescribing the group-to-group mass of the plan) is clean, flexible, and modular, and the derivation of the FairSinkhorn update via first-order conditions (Proposition 3.3/Appendix A.1) is technically correct and yields a natural, easy-to-implement block-scaling modification of Sinkhorn.

The two relaxation strategies (convex penalization vs. bilevel cost learning) are sensibly chosen and their qualitative trade-offs (convexity vs. flexibility/reusability) are articulated reasonably in Section 4.3.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical guarantee for cost learning is overstated and effectively vacuous. Theorem 4.4 only controls the deviation between the finite-sample and population fairness losses, with an exp(5 R_Theta / eps) factor. For the neural cost and any practical epsilon this factor is astronomically large, so the bound does not 'guarantee that the learned cost yields fair matchings on unseen data' as claimed in the abstract/contributions. The theorem also says nothing about the level of fairness attained (both plans could be arbitrarily unfair); it is a concentration bound, not a fairness guarantee. This directly undercuts a central claim.

The paper is internally inconsistent about its own guarantees: the abstract/contributions claim a bound 'guaranteeing that the learned cost yields fair matchings on unseen data,' yet the conclusion states 'Deriving a generalization bound for the cost learning approach is left for future work.' These cannot both be true, and it is unclear what the actual contribution is.

The sample-complexity result (Theorem 4.2) is not verifiable from the manuscript. Appendix B.2 is garbled (e.g., 'O(1/sqrt(n)^{-1})', truncated Lemma B.2 proof, a referenced 'Theorem B.4' that is never stated, and a hand-waved appeal to a 'generalization of Theorem 6 from [58]' to absorb the penalty term). The claimed 'novel' bound appears to reduce directly to existing entropic-OT sample complexity with an extra log factor, so the 'independent interest' claim is not substantiated.

The FairSinkhorn convergence claim is unsupported. Remark 1 asserts convergence by citing Benamou et al. [4] because the algorithm 'alternates between projections on sets defined by linear constraints,' but no convergence proof, fixed-point characterization, or rate is given, and no complexity/efficiency analysis backs the 'efficiently' claim in the abstract. There is also an unaddressed feasibility issue: F is defined via population group marginals p, q, whereas Problem (3) uses empirical marginals 1/n, 1/m; if the empirical group frequencies differ from p, q the fairness constraints may be infeasible and the block-scaling step can diverge. This is never discussed.

The empirical evaluation is too thin to support the claims. Only two synthetic 2D datasets (Gaussians, concentric circles) are used, with 20 points per subgroup; there are no real-world datasets, no comparison against any prior fairness-in-matching method, and the 'metrics' (KL between plans, cost difference) are defined relative to unfaired Sinkhorn rather than to any external baseline. The reusability study (Fig. 7) only compares running times at a single hand-tuned operating point.

The presentation contains clear errors that impede reading: subsections 5.1 and 5.2 are duplicated verbatim under the same title; experiments cite 'Theorem 4.1' and 'Theorem 4.2' for Mahalanobis/neural costs when these are actually Examples 4.1/4.2; Figure 5's caption describes '2D gaussians' for the concentric-circles data; the appendix is full of LaTeX artifacts and missing content. These go beyond cosmetics because they make the theoretical claims hard to check.

Several claims in the introduction are unsupported by the evidence presented (e.g., that FairSinkhorn computes 'perfectly fair transport plans efficiently,' and that the penalty 'does not worsen statistical efficiency' is asserted from an unverifiable proof). The overall framing overstates both the novelty (the F-fair constraint is a fairly direct group-marginal constraint on the coupling) and the strength of the results.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated notion of group fairness for optimal transport: a central planner specifies a target matrix F of inter-group matching probabilities, which is flexible enough to encode anti-homogamy goals, quotas, and diversity objectives. This is a genuinely new framing for fairness in matching via OT.

The FairSinkhorn derivation (Proposition 3.3) is clean: the fairness constraints are linear, so the Lagrangian yields a multiplicative update that extends Sinkhorn with an additional group-level projection step. The construction is intuitive and directly implementable.

Two complementary relaxation strategies are thoughtfully contrasted (convex penalized OT vs. bilevel cost learning), with an explicit and useful discussion of their trade-offs (convexity, flexibility/interpretability, reusability).

The sample-complexity result for fairness-penalized entropic OT (Theorem 4.2) recovers the 1/sqrt(n) rate of standard entropic OT and is argued to generalize to arbitrary convex penalties, which is a plausible contribution of independent interest.

The deviation bound (Theorem 4.4) holds uniformly over the cost parameter family, which does provide a sensible reusability argument: if training fairness is small, measured fairness on fresh samples stays close to the population value.
The paper is honest about limitations, explicitly flagging that a generalization bound for the cost-learning approach is left for future work.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is entirely synthetic and very small-scale (n_x = n_y = 20 samples per subgroup; ~40-120 points; reusability on 50 samples per subgroup). Despite motivating the work with concrete matching applications (school assignment, dating, kidney exchange), no real matching dataset is used, so practical significance is not convincingly demonstrated.

Presentation problems: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 are duplicated verbatim under the same heading ('Approaches and Metrics'), and the text repeatedly cites Examples 4.1/4.2 as 'Theorem 4.1/4.2'. There are also minor notation inconsistencies (K_epsilon vs K_s; 'sv' vs 'sw'), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The abstract claims a bound 'guaranteeing that the learned cost yields fair matchings on unseen data', but Theorem 4.4 only bounds the difference between finite-sample and population fairness for a fixed cost; it is conditional on the training fairness being small and does not itself establish that the learned cost generalizes well. The claim is somewhat stronger than what is proven.

The deviation bound exp(5 R_Theta / epsilon) / sqrt(n) is exponentially loose in 1/epsilon, which substantially limits its practical relevance in the small-regularization regime that is often of interest. The authors note this is unavoidable in the worst case, but the practical bite is limited.

FairSinkhorn convergence is asserted only by citation to [4] (iterative Bregman projections); no convergence proof or rate is provided, and the alternating multiplicative-update scheme is not rigorously shown to converge to the intersection of the marginal and fairness constraint sets.
No comparison against existing fair matching or constrained-OT baselines; the empirical comparison is limited to plain Sinkhorn and the authors' own FairSinkhorn.
Reproducibility is partial: code is only promised 'upon publication', and the garbled proof appendix makes independent verification of the central theoretical results difficult.

strengths: Introduces a novel and flexible notion of group fairness for optimal transport: a fairness target matrix F specifies desired group-level matching probabilities, naturally accommodating quotas, homogamy limits, and diversity goals (Examples 3.1–3.2, Remark 3.1).

Provides FairSinkhorn, a simple Sinkhorn-type modification for exact fair OT, derived from first-order conditions (Prop. 3.3), and shows empirically comparable convergence to standard Sinkhorn (Fig. 7a).

Proposes two practical relaxations: a convex penalized OT problem solved via generalized conditional gradient, and a bilevel cost-learning approach that yields reusable cost functions, with a clear comparison of their trade-offs (Sec. 4.3).

Establishes finite-sample guarantees: an O(1/sqrt(n)) sample-complexity bound for penalized entropic OT (Thm. 4.2) and a uniform fairness-deviation bound for parameterized learned costs (Thm. 4.4), extending existing statistical OT results.

Experiments on synthetic Gaussian/Circles data and a semi-synthetic dating-app dataset illustrate the cost-fairness trade-off, reusability of learned costs, and fairness generalization to new samples (Figs. 3–5).
Includes a thoughtful limitations and impact statement, correctly framing the choice of fairness targets as a political/ethical decision rather than a purely technical one.
weaknesses: FairSinkhorn lacks a convergence proof or fixed-point analysis; the paper only establishes first-order optimality conditions and empirical convergence, so the claim of efficiently computing perfectly fair plans is not theoretically guaranteed. Handling of infeasible finite-sample targets and division by zero when F_{sw}=0 is also not discussed.
Exact fairness may be infeasible for empirical marginals when the target F is feasible only for population marginals, a practical issue that is not addressed.

Empirical evaluation is limited to synthetic and semi-synthetic data, with no comparison to prior fair matching or fair OT methods (e.g., constrained OT, fair Wasserstein barycenter, or other fair matching baselines); only vanilla OT serves as a baseline, weakening claims of effectiveness.

Theoretical bounds carry exponential dependence on ε and λ (penalized OT) or R_Θ/ε (cost learning), and the cost-learning bound does not account for non-convex bilevel optimization error, limiting practical relevance.

Presentation issues: theorem statements contain typos (e.g., O(1/sqrt(n)^{-1})), notation is occasionally inconsistent (F_{sv} vs F_{sw}, integral notation in Thm. 4.4), the code URL is missing, and some extracted tables appear corrupted/unreadable.
The fairness target is assumed given; there is no guidance or sensitivity analysis on choosing F, and experiments use a single arbitrary target per dataset.

strengths: Introduces a clean, well-motivated and flexible notion of group fairness for OT: an F-fair coupling is one whose induced group-level coupling equals a prescribed target F in Π(p,q). The formulation naturally accommodates quotas, homogamy limits, and policy rules (four-fifths rule, EU board quotas), and the reduction of exact fairness to linear constraints on the plan is elegant.

The FairSinkhorn algorithm follows naturally from first-order optimality conditions (Prop. 3.3), and existence/uniqueness of the F-fair plan is established (Prop. 3.2) via a constructive product coupling and compactness/strict-convexity arguments that look correct.

Provides two complementary relaxations with theory: a convex penalized OT with a sample-complexity bound matching the O(1/√n) entropic-OT rate (Thm 4.2), and a bilevel cost-learning approach with a uniform-in-θ fairness deviation bound (Thm 4.4). The claim that the penalty does not degrade statistical efficiency is a reasonable and useful result.

Good practical framing: the cost-learning approach is reusable on unseen samples, and the interpretability of the Mahalanobis parametrization is a nice touch. Code is released and implementation details are documented.
Honest limitations section and a thoughtful impact statement that correctly stresses that the fairness target is a political/ethical decision and that OT is only an abstraction of real matching.
weaknesses: Convergence of FairSinkhorn—the paper's first and central algorithmic contribution—is never proven. The iteration is only compared to standard Sinkhorn empirically (Fig. 7a). For a constrained fixed-point/scaling scheme, convergence is not automatic, so the claim that it 'computes perfectly fair transport plans efficiently' rests on a heuristic.

The theoretical contributions are largely incremental extensions of known results via standard techniques: the penalized-OT bound linearizes the convex penalty (Rakotomamonjy et al., 2015) and reduces to Genevay (2019)/Mena & Niles-Weed entropic-OT rates, while Thm 4.4 rescales Rigollet & Stromme (2025, Thm 6) to bounded parametrized costs. The paper itself concedes the exponential dependence in ε and λ is inherited, so the 'novel sample complexity bound' is modest in substance.

Theorem 4.4's bound carries an exp(5R_Θ/ε) factor; for the neural cost with Lipschitz constant C_Θ this is enormous and the bound is practically vacuous. The paper notes the exponential ε-dependence is 'unavoidable in the worst case' but does not discuss the practical implications for the cost-learning method it motivates.

Empirical evaluation is thin: only synthetic Gaussians/circles and a semi-synthetic dating dataset, with vanilla OT as the sole baseline. There is no comparison to the closest related method (Nguyen et al., 2025) or to other fairness-aware matching approaches, and no real-world matching benchmark, so the practical value of the framework is not convincingly demonstrated.

Technical presentation contains sloppiness that hinders verification: repeated typographical errors such as O(1/√n^{-1}) in Thm 4.2, and the proof of Thm 4.2 relies on a 'Theorem C.4' (sub-Gaussian concentration) that is referenced but not stated in the provided appendix, making the key step hard to check.

The fairness target must be supplied by a central planner and must be a valid coupling of the group marginals; the sensitivity of the methods to target misspecification or to infeasible/partially specified targets is not studied, despite being central to deployment.

strengths: Introduces a novel and flexible group fairness notion for optimal transport: a fairness target F as a coupling between sensitive groups, enabling quotas, homogamy limits, and regulatory targets. The motivation and examples (school assignment, four-fifths rule, EU directive) are compelling.

Provides an elegant dual characterization of exact fair entropic OT (Π = diag(e^{f/ε})(K⊙H)diag(e^{g/ε})) leading to FairSinkhorn, a simple modification of Sinkhorn. The derivation is clean and the algorithm is empirically shown to converge at a rate similar to standard Sinkhorn.

Proposes two well-motivated relaxations: convex penalized OT solved via generalized conditional gradient, and a bilevel cost-learning approach that yields a reusable cost function. The trade-offs between exact and relaxed fairness are clearly illustrated.

Establishes nontrivial theoretical results: Theorem 4.2 gives O(1/√n) sample complexity for penalized entropic OT, matching standard entropic OT; Theorem 4.4 gives a uniform-in-θ deviation bound for finite-sample fairness under parameterized costs, extending Rigollet & Stromme (2025). Proof sketches and appendix details are provided.

Experiments on synthetic Gaussian/Circles and a semi-synthetic dating-app dataset demonstrate the cost-fairness trade-off, reusability of learned costs, faster inference, and generalization to new samples. Additional appendix experiments address deterministic sampling and convergence speed.
The paper includes an honest limitations discussion and ethics statement, acknowledging that the fairness target is a political choice and that OT abstracts away real-world matching complexities.
weaknesses: FairSinkhorn lacks a convergence proof and convergence rate. The paper only empirically compares its convergence to Sinkhorn (Appendix D.5). For an algorithm intended to compute exact fair transport plans, a theoretical guarantee (e.g., conditions under which the alternating updates converge to the unique optimum) would strengthen the central claim. Feasibility of the exact target F with empirical marginals is also not discussed: if F is specified at the population level but does not satisfy the empirical row/column sums, the finite-sample constraints may be infeasible. In the synthetic setup, F = [[0.20,0.30],[0.28,0.22]] has column sums 0.48/0.52 despite the text stating sensitive attributes are balanced, which is a reproducibility concern.

The theoretical contributions are somewhat incremental and come with strong caveats. Theorem 4.2 extends known entropic OT sample complexity via linearization and inherits exponential dependence in ε and λ, limiting practical relevance. Theorem 4.4 bounds finite-sample estimation error for a fixed cost parameter θ, not the generalization error of the learned θ to unseen data; the abstract's claim about matching unseen data is therefore overstated. The bilevel outer problem is nonconvex and no optimization guarantees are provided.

The experimental evaluation is limited: only two synthetic datasets and one semi-synthetic dating-app dataset are used. There are no real-world matching experiments and no comparisons to alternative fairness-constrained OT or fair bipartite matching baselines. Several trade-off curves appear to lack error bars or statistical tests, and scalability to large-scale matching problems is not demonstrated.

There are presentation and notation issues that reduce clarity: e.g., the experiments refer to 'Theorem 4.1' and 'Theorem 4.2' when they mean Examples 4.1 and 4.2; Appendix C uses 'O(1/√n^{-1})' and 'exp(5RΘ)ε^{-1}' instead of O(1/√n) and exp(5RΘ/ε); 'F_{sv}' appears for 'F_{sw}'; and 'Theorem C.4' is referenced but not clearly present. Some experimental details (random seeds for the main trade-off plots, full construction of the fairness target) are missing, slightly hindering reproducibility.
